title: The car that drives itself

fn.en: Talk about machines in our lives; add and single out information.

can.en: I can add extra information to a sentence and single out exactly which thing I mean.

rc: the present perfect against the past simple

acts.say: Say which of these you would actually trust.

Parking itself by the side of the road.

sub.en: Does the clause tell you WHICH one, or does it just add extra information?

items.q: This is the car ___ drives itself.
items.why: A defining clause about a thing takes that or which. what is never a relative pronoun here.

items.q: Google’s car, ___ has now driven a million kilometres, sticks to the speed limit.
items.why: A non-defining clause always takes which, never that, and always has commas.

items.q: Only people ___ skills are better than the machine’s will have work.
The engineer ___ designed it started as a taxi driver.
That is the reason ___ so many accidents happen at junctions.
Ninety per cent of accidents are caused by human error, ___ is the whole argument for driverless cars.
items.why: Here which refers back to the whole idea in the first clause, not to one noun.

items.q: The phone ___ I bought last year is already out of date.
items.why: In a defining clause, the object pronoun can be left out: the phone I bought.

items.q: My sister, ___ has never driven, thinks the whole idea is mad.

rows: This is the car that drives itself.
The engineer who designed it was a taxi driver.
The phone I bought is out of date.
People whose skills are high will have work.
Google’s car, which cost millions, sticks to the limit.
Most crashes are human error, which is the point.

lines: This is the car [that|who|what] parks itself.
Google’s car, [which|that|what] has now driven a million kilometres, has never had a speeding fine.
Only people [whose|who’s|which] skills are better than the machines’ will have work.
The engineer [who|which|whose] designed it [started|has started|was starting] as a taxi driver.
Ninety per cent of crashes are caused by human error, [which|that|what] is exactly the point.

items.cue: Rewrite it with WHOSE. Begin: The workers…

items.a: That is the thing that worries me most

items.why: what is never used as a relative pronoun. Use that or which.

w: , that has driven a million kilometres,
items.fix: , which has driven a million kilometres,
items.why: A non-defining clause takes which, never that.

w: My sister who has never driven
items.fix: My sister, who has never driven,
items.why: Extra information needs commas on both sides.
The relative pronoun already is the object — do not repeat it with it.

acts.title: The car that drives itself
text: A driver on a busy motorway presses a button on the steering wheel, and the car takes over. It is not science fiction. Driverless cars, which have now covered millions of kilometres in California, are already on the roads.

Most of the pieces have been in ordinary cars for years. A car that brakes automatically when the vehicle in front slows down is nothing unusual. Nor is one that parks itself, or one that warns the driver who is slipping out of the correct lane. Going fully driverless is simply the next step.

The cars come with fast broadband, which allows them to overtake safely and even to talk to the traffic lights as they approach a junction. Traffic jams, which cost the average commuter a working week every year, could disappear, because cars that can talk to each other are able to drive at speed much closer together.

The argument that convinces most people is a simpler one. More than fifty million people are killed or injured on the roads every year, and around ninety per cent of those accidents are caused by human error. A machine sticks to the speed limit, does not get tired and has never yet been in a hurry.

There is one group for whom the change is not a convenience but a door opening. People whose disability has always made an ordinary driving test impossible have spent their whole lives depending on somebody else. For them, a car that drives itself is not a gadget. It is the difference between asking for a lift and going out.

tts: Intelligent machines that can serve us in supermarkets, give us directions and even drive for us are becoming part of all our lives.
Some of the things machines can do now would have seemed impossible just a few years ago. And there is more to come.
Amazon promises robot drones which will deliver our packages, and Rolls-Royce says robo-ships, which won’t need any crew, will soon be sailing our seas.
But what will this mean for our workers?
Some think that only people whose skills are better than the machines’ abilities will have work.
Those who don’t have high-level skills risk being unemployable, or will have to work for very low wages.

write.q: Write about one machine or device that has changed your daily life. Use at least two defining relative clauses (which one you mean) and one non-defining clause with commas (extra information).
write.ph: The device that changed my week most is…
plan: which device, and why that one
what it does that nothing else does
write.model: The device that changed my week most is not my phone but the small electric kettle in the office, which somebody bought out of their own money in 2021. It boils in forty seconds, which means nobody stands about waiting any more. The colleague who bought it, who has since left the company, never told anybody how much it cost. The thing that surprises me is how quickly it stopped feeling like a luxury. That is probably the reason why people who complain about new technology are usually complaining about something they already depend on.

speak.q: Describe two machines out loud: one you would not give up, and one you think is unnecessary. Say exactly which one you mean, then add one extra fact about it.
speak.model: The one I wouldn’t give up is the washing machine — the one in the flat, which my landlord bought second-hand and which has never once broken down. The thing that makes it good is that it’s quiet. The one I think is unnecessary is the smart speaker my brother gave me, which mostly sits there telling me the weather I can see from the window.
